title: Common Design Anti-Patterns
summary: Structural, architecture-level bad practices bigger than any single smelly method — God Object, tight coupling, spaghetti code, magic numbers — and why they accrete over time.

slides.markdown:
Where a code smell is local — one method, one class — a **design anti-pattern** is structural: a recurring bad solution at the architecture level that emerges from many individually-reasonable decisions. Nobody sets out to build a God Object; it accretes one "just add it here, it's easiest" commit at a time.

This topic covers the anti-patterns you'll recognize in real codebases and in interviews: God Object, tight coupling, spaghetti code, and magic numbers — plus how they differ from the smells in [Common Code Smells](common-code-smells).

slides.sectionTitle: God Object: one class that knows and does too much
slides.markdown:
A **God Object** is a single class that has become the hub for most of a system's logic — it knows about orders, users, payments, and notifications, and half the codebase imports it. It rarely starts that way: each feature adds "just one more responsibility" to the class that's already easiest to reach from everywhere, because it's already central.

The cost compounds: every change risks touching unrelated behavior, every test needs to mock half the system, and no single engineer can hold the whole class's behavior in their head. By the time it's recognized, splitting it apart is a multi-week project — which is exactly why catching the Large Class smell early (see [Common Code Smells](common-code-smells)) matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a God Object's dependencies fanning out
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a single central class labelled OrderManager drawn as a large hub in the middle, with roughly a dozen thin arrows fanning out to and from smaller boxes around it labelled PaymentService, EmailSender, InventoryService, UserProfile, ReportGenerator, AuditLog, ShippingCalculator, and a mobile API controller — every arrow touching the same central box >>>

Every box on the diagram depends on the same central class, and the central class depends back on most of them. That density is the visual signature of a God Object: there's no seam left to change one thing without a ripple.

Compare it mentally to a healthy dependency graph — a few arrows per box, mostly one direction — and the difference in "blast radius" per change becomes obvious.

slides.sectionTitle: Tight coupling: symptoms you can point to
slides.markdown:
**Tight coupling** means two classes know too much about each other's internals — one reaches into the other's fields, calls its private helper logic indirectly, or assumes a specific implementation instead of a contract. The symptom is concrete: you can't change `PaymentProcessor`'s internal retry logic without also editing `OrderService`, `RefundService`, and the admin dashboard, because all three were written against its internals rather than a stable interface.

The practical test: count how many other files break when you change one class's implementation but keep its public behavior the same. If the number is more than one or two, the coupling is tighter than the design should allow.

slides.sectionTitle: Spaghetti code and the missing-architecture smell
slides.markdown:
**Spaghetti code** is what you get when control flow and dependencies form no discernible layering — a UI event handler directly runs a SQL query, a background job calls into request-handling code, and tracing "what happens when a user clicks submit" means jumping through a dozen files with no consistent direction.

It's usually not one bad decision but the *absence* of an architectural decision: nobody defined which layer is allowed to call which, so every shortcut that shipped a feature faster became a permanent path. The fix is rarely a full rewrite — it's introducing boundaries (a service layer, a clear data-access layer) and enforcing that new code respects them, even while old spaghetti gets untangled gradually.

A **magic number** or **magic string** is a literal value with meaning baked into the code with no name attached — `if (status == 3)`, `if (role == "A")`. The reader has no way to know what `3` or `"A"` mean without hunting down every other place that number appears, and if the meaning ever needs to change, every occurrence is a place to miss.

The fix is cheap and high-leverage compared to most anti-pattern fixes: name it — a constant, an enum member (`Status.SHIPPED`), a well-named config value. It doesn't remove complexity, but it makes the complexity visible instead of hidden in a literal, which is most of why magic values rot maintainability over time.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: decomposing a God Object into cohesive collaborators

slides.markdown:
The two terms overlap in spirit — both are "a signal something is wrong" — but they operate at different scopes.

| | Code smell | Design anti-pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Local — one method or class | Structural — spans classes, modules, or the whole system |
| Detected by | Reading one file | Reading the dependency graph, or feeling the pain of a cross-cutting change |
| Example | Long method, feature envy | God Object, tight coupling, spaghetti code |
| Typical fix cost | Minutes to an hour — Extract Method, rename | Days to weeks — introduce seams, split responsibilities |

**How to decide which term to use:** if you can point at a single method and say "this is the problem," it's a smell; if fixing it means touching how multiple classes relate to each other, call it an anti-pattern.

**Wrong belief:** "This class is 800 lines, so it must be a God Object and needs splitting."

**Why it's wrong:** size alone isn't the diagnostic — a large class that does *one* cohesive thing, like a state machine with many well-organized transition cases, or a legitimate coordinator whose job really is to orchestrate many steps of one workflow, is not automatically an anti-pattern. Splitting it just to hit a line-count target can scatter one coherent concept across five files, making it harder to follow, not easier.

**Correct model:** ask whether the class has multiple *unrelated* responsibilities (the God Object test) rather than whether it's merely long. A big class with one job and clear internal structure can be legitimate; a small class doing three unrelated jobs is still an anti-pattern.

slides.sectionTitle: Interview framing: "tell me about the messiest code you've worked in"
slides.markdown:
This question is really asking two things at once: can you diagnose a real anti-pattern precisely, and did you actually improve it, or just complain about it? A weak answer stays vague ("it was really messy and hard to work with"). A strong answer names the specific anti-pattern — "a God Object that every service imported for user data" — and the concrete symptom that made it painful, like a one-line feature taking three days because of hidden coupling.

The structure that lands well: name the anti-pattern, describe the specific pain it caused, describe the concrete step you or the team took (even a partial one, like introducing an interface at the seam), and be honest if it was never fully fixed — interviewers trust "we contained it" more than an implausibly tidy resolution.
